title: Client-side chunking: latency vs cost field notes
content:
Summary:

Short: early field notes on how pushing chunking decisions to the client (vs server-side chunking) changes observed p50/p90/p99 latency and per-query cost under a streaming decode workload. Useful for deciding defaults in the SDK (chunk size, max inflight chunks) and for guidance in the Console docs.

Why this experiment: we keep seeing customers toggle client chunking to reduce server CPU pressure, but effects on tail latency and token-unit cost are noisy. This doc collects quick runs, heuristics, and open questions.

Test setup (lightweight):
- Date: 2029-06-14 to 2029-06-17 (runs repeated at different hours)
- Region: us-west-2 (single AZ to avoid multi-region noise)
- Model config: rwd-13b-int4 (production-ish profile) and rwd-7b-fp16 (control)
- Client: nodejs SDK v2.4 (instrumented to measure chunk boundaries, network RTT)
- Server: Redwood hosted inference pool with streaming endpoint, standard batching pipeline
- Workload: chat-like streaming responses, avg prompt 45 tokens, response target 160 tokens (sampled top-k)
- Concurrency: 60 simulated users, sessionized (keep-alive sockets), each issues 1 request per 30s on average
- Measured: client-observed end-to-end latency (first byte, last byte), server token compute time, server CPU utilization, tokens-per-request, cost-per-request (server CPU+gpu rough cost model), p50/p90/p99 latencies

Variants tested (key knobs):
A) Server-side chunking (baseline): server controls what size chunks to stream to client; network sends bigger frames but fewer frames overall
B) Client-side chunking small (client requests 8-token frames)
C) Client-side chunking medium (client requests 32-token frames)
D) Client-side chunking large (client requests 128-token frames)
E) Client-side chunking + max-inflight=1 vs max-inflight=4

Quick high-level findings:
- Small client chunk sizes (8 tokens) decrease server-side memory/KV pressure slightly (because server can flush earlier) but increase CPU overhead and per-query throughput cost by ~ 8-12% in our rough cost model due to more frequent scheduling and RPC overhead.
- p50 not strongly affected across variants. p90 increases modestly for small-chunk client-side (about +20–30ms), p99 increases noticeably (about +80–160ms) depending on inflight concurrency.
- Medium chunking (32 tokens) is a sweet spot for this workload: similar cost to server-side baseline (within ±2–4%), p90 near baseline, p99 modestly higher (~+40ms).
- Large client chunking (128 tokens) reduces per-request CPU overhead slightly (fewer RPCs) but increases the perceived first-byte latency for streaming use cases (user waits longer before seeing content). Not acceptable for low-latency UX.
- Allowing multiple inflight chunk requests (max-inflight=4) with small chunk sizes recovers tail latency but at the expense of higher concurrency on server slots and slightly higher amortized cost per token (due to less efficient batching).

Representative ASCII tables (median of several runs):

1) p50/p90/p99 (ms) — end-to-end last-byte latency by variant (rwd-13b-int4)

| Variant           | p50  | p90  | p99  | notes                               |
|-------------------|------|------|------|-------------------------------------|
| Server-chunking   | 210  | 310  | 480  | baseline                            |
| Client-8-token    | 220  | 345  | 640  | single-inflight                      |
| Client-32-token   | 215  | 325  | 520  | balanced                            |
| Client-128-token  | 260  | 360  | 530  | high first-byte wait                |
| Client-8x-inflight| 230  | 320  | 500  | 8-token with inflight=4             |

2) Rough cost per request (amortized cents) — compute+rpc cost model (not including infra overheads)

| Variant           | tokens | compute-ms | cost-cents | relative |
|-------------------|--------|------------|------------|----------|
| Server-chunking   | 160    | 180        | 0.36       | 1.00x    |
| Client-8-token    | 160    | 198        | 0.40       | 1.11x    |
| Client-32-token   | 160    | 182        | 0.37       | 1.03x    |
| Client-128-token  | 160    | 176        | 0.35       | 0.97x    |
| Client-8x-inflight| 160    | 202        | 0.41       | 1.14x    |
Notes on numbers: these are drawn from host CPU time + RPC count impact. GPU token time unchanged (model decoding same), but CPU scheduling, IPC and RPC overheads add up. Cost model here is intentionally simple: $0.002 per compute-ms + $0.001 per RPC-call-equivalent. Use just to compare variants.

Observations and interpretation:
- UX vs cost tradeoff: small chunks with single inflight give earlier streaming updates (smaller first-byte? actually opposite — more frequent bytes but each chunk small) but hurt tail because scheduling overhead causes jitter; inflight parallelism helps tail but increases slot pressure. For chat UX, first-byte time matters a lot — so large chunk sizes (server-side or 32-token) often preferred.
- Server-side chunking can make smarter coalescing decisions because it sees global batching opportunities; client-side chunking hides that from server and increases number of RPC boundaries.
- The ideal defaults depend on the surface: SDKs for UX-focused apps (chat apps) should default to client chunk size ~32 tokens and max-inflight=1 or 2; SDKs for heavy-throughput embedding/analysis apps should default to larger chunk sizes or server-managed chunking.
- Edge cases: when network RTT is high (>80ms), multiple small in-flight chunks mask RTT and improve perceived latency despite cost. We should add RTT-aware heuristics.

Visual sketch (timeline, conceptual):
- Client requests chunk N -> server schedules a decode window -> server replies with chunk bytes -> client immediately requests next chunk.
- More frequent small requests raise server QPS on control path (scheduling RPCs), reduce ability to batch tokens in the server pipeline.

Open questions / followups (next runs):
- Repeat experiments cross-region (us-east-1 and eu-west-1) to capture RTT sensitivity.
- Run with rwd-70b-quantized to measure effect when per-token GPU cost dominates vs CPU overhead. Hypothesis: client-side chunking overhead is less visible when GPU token cost is >> CPU scheduling cost.
- Sweep max-inflight values (1,2,4,8) with small chunk sizes under varying concurrency (20, 60, 200 users).
- Measure memory/KV pressure more directly (instrument Redis/KV cache eviction and server slot memory).
- Try hybrid approach: server suggests a chunk size per-session (initial probe) based on model and observed RTT.

Decision guidance (draft for Console/SDK docs):
- Default behavior (recommended): client chunk size = 32 tokens, max-inflight = 1. Rationale: balance of UX (smooth streaming) and cost (near baseline).
- Advanced: if client detects RTT > 80ms, increase max-inflight to 2 automatically.
- For throughput/analysis endpoints (non-interactive): prefer server-side or large chunk sizes (>=128 tokens) to minimize RPCs and cost.

Implementation notes for SDK owners:
- Expose chunkSize and maxInflight as top-level options with clear UX wording.
- Telemetry: emit metrics for chunk-size distribution, per-request RPC count, and server-surface batching efficiency (approx by server compute-ms / tokens).
- Console: add a tooltip in model details that explains chunking tradeoffs and offers a one-click "suggest optimal for chat" setting that applies 32/1.

Appendix: sample log snippet (client-side, small-chunk run)

[client] 2029-06-15T16:23:02.112Z request-id=abc123 chunk=1 req=8 bytes=64 rtt=43ms
[server] 2029-06-15T16:23:02.118Z request-id=abc123 schedule-start slot=slot-7 queue-len=12
[server] 2029-06-15T16:23:02.300Z request-id=abc123 chunk=1 done compute-ms=48
[client] 2029-06-15T16:23:02.305Z request-id=abc123 chunk=2 req=8 bytes=80 rtt=43ms

Small random notes to self:
- Watch for GC pauses on node client when chunk callback frequency is high — saw one flake where client paused ~40ms at p95.
- Talk to serving-runtime about adding an advisory header: "suggested-chunk=32" so server can provide hints. Avoid hard binding; client can still override.

Next steps owner: Ravi to run RTT sweep (EU + APAC), Eva to prototype suggest-chunk header, Maya to draft Console copy and SDK PR text.

End of field notes.
